newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ expects c/a surplus to decline more slowly.
newsitem.headline: BOJ expects c/a surplus to decline more slowly.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus is still on a declining trend, but the tempo of the decline will slow, a report by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) said on Tuesday.
"We expect the speed of shrinkage in the surplus to become more gradual compared with the rapid drop we saw from the latter half of 1995 to the first half of 1996," it said.

Machinery exports for capital investment are unlikely to drop drastically, as they are helped by good economic performances in the United States and Asia. Prospects are becoming brighter for the auto industry, helped by a recovery in U.S. demand and progress in stock adjustments, it said.
For the semiconductor industry, sharp drops in prices have subsided and the pace of the decline has become more mild. The weaker yen would also help boost exports, it said.
"We think net exports, which are now showing little growth, will in the future show a gradual increasing trend," it said.
Meanwhile, net imports are likely to continue strong growth as domestic demand improves and Japanese companies stick to their plans to shift production overseas.
But the boom in demand for personal computers was likely to moderate and the weaker yen would also suppress a flood of imports, it said.
Depending on future currency movements, companies may also slow the pace of moving their production overseas, it said.

The sharp fall in the current account surplus, which came amid structural changes, has been a factor slowing down the pace of Japan's economic recovery, and some have voiced worries that it may even have a negative impact, the report said.
But rises in imports reflect a rebound in domestic demand and a weaker yen, which helped to brighten business sentiment, was a product of falling surpluses, it said.
"There is little possibility that a shrinking surplus would hinder economic recovery," a BOJ official said.
